raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a catheter-based strategy to reduce thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation (AF) by excluding the dominant site of cardiac thrombus formation in non-valvular AF. The rationale is anatomical and pathophysiological: the left atrial appendage (LAA) has complex trabeculated morphology, variable lobes, and contractile dysfunction during AF, promoting stasis and thrombus; early surgical and pathological observations linked appendage obliteration with stroke prevention concepts [1], [2]. LAAC is therefore best understood not as systemic anticoagulation “replacement” for all mechanisms of stroke, but as a targeted mechanical intervention for LAA-mediated embolism.

The field evolved from feasibility experience with the PLAATO device to randomized evidence with endocardial nitinol devices. PLAATO established that transseptal LAA exclusion was technically feasible in high-risk patients unsuitable for warfarin, although that platform was discontinued [3], [4]. The WATCHMAN device then provided the first pivotal randomized data. In PROTECT AF, LAAC was non-inferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, but early procedural complications—particularly pericardial effusion—tempered enthusiasm [5]. Longer follow-up confirmed durable efficacy signals and declining event rates after the periprocedural period [6]. PREVAIL, designed partly to address safety and reproducibility, showed improved procedural safety but did not meet all efficacy non-inferiority criteria, in part because of unexpectedly low ischemic stroke rates in the warfarin arm [7]. Patient-level 5-year analyses of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL suggested comparable stroke/systemic embolism prevention versus warfarin, with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, cardiovascular death, and post-procedure bleeding [8].

LAAC is used most often in patients with elevated thromboembolic risk and an unfavorable long-term anticoagulation profile. The ASAP study supported WATCHMAN implantation without a warfarin transition in patients considered ineligible for warfarin, using antiplatelet-based therapy [9]. Large registries subsequently demonstrated high implant success in broader and older populations. EWOLUTION reported high procedural success and acceptable early and 1-year outcomes despite frequent contraindications to oral anticoagulation [10], [11]. In the United States, the NCDR LAAO Registry showed that postapproval practice involved older, comorbid patients with high CHA₂DS₂-VASc and HAS-BLED scores, while major in-hospital adverse events were uncommon but not negligible [12], [13].

Device technology has changed substantially. WATCHMAN FLX was designed to improve recapturability, sealing, and safety; PINNACLE FLX reported high closure rates and low serious procedure-related events in a prospective single-arm approval study [14]. Parallel development of the Amplatzer Cardiac Plug/Amulet family emphasized a lobe-and-disc design. The global Amulet observational program showed high implant success and acceptable 1-year outcomes [15], [16]. In Amulet IDE, Amulet was non-inferior to WATCHMAN for safety and effectiveness and superior for LAA closure, although procedure-related complications were more frequent [17]. SWISS-APERO, a randomized imaging-focused comparison, reinforced that device selection affects residual patency, leak profile, and procedural trade-offs [18].

The most clinically relevant comparator has shifted from warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk AF patients to LAAC or DOACs and showed non-inferiority for a composite of cardioembolic events, cardiovascular death, bleeding, and device/procedure complications, with sustained 4-year results [19], [20]. OPTION extended the question to patients after AF ablation, showing LAAC was non-inferior to oral anticoagulation for death, stroke, or systemic embolism and reduced nonprocedural clinically relevant bleeding [21]. More recent randomized data are nuanced: CLOSURE-AF, in high-risk German patients, did not demonstrate non-inferiority of LAAC versus physician-directed medical therapy [22], whereas CHAMPION-AF suggested WATCHMAN FLX was non-inferior to DOAC therapy for cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism in anticoagulation-eligible patients, with less nonprocedural bleeding but ongoing debate regarding ischemic stroke signals and patient selection [23].

Complications and surveillance remain central. Device-related thrombus occurs in a minority but is associated with thromboembolic events and usually prompts temporary anticoagulation [24], [25]. Peridevice leak is common by sensitive imaging, but its clinical implications vary by size, timing, device, and imaging modality; long-term analyses suggest small leaks may not be benign in all settings [26]. Postimplant antithrombotic therapy is heterogeneous, balancing endothelialization, device thrombosis, and bleeding; registry analyses suggest practice is moving from warfarin-based protocols toward DOAC-only, DOAC-plus-aspirin, and antiplatelet strategies, but randomized regimen trials remain limited [27].

Current consensus documents and AF guidelines position percutaneous LAAC as reasonable for patients with AF at increased stroke risk who have contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation, and as a potential alternative in selected patients with high bleeding risk or strong preference after shared decision-making [28], [29]. The essential clinical task is careful selection: confirming non-valvular AF stroke risk, clarifying whether bleeding risk is modifiable, excluding LAA thrombus, choosing device and imaging strategy according to anatomy, and planning surveillance and antithrombotic therapy [30]. The future of LAAC will depend on longer DOAC-era follow-up, better risk models for residual non-LAA stroke, strategies to prevent device-related thrombus and leak, and transparent interpretation of industry-sponsored trials.
